rule.title: The Four Tones of Mandarin
rule.explanation: Mandarin has 4 tones that change the meaning of a word. Tone 1 (ā) is high and flat. Tone 2 (á) rises like asking a question. Tone 3 (ǎ) dips down then up. Tone 4 (à) falls sharply. Getting tones right is essential — the wrong tone means a completely different word!

rule.title: Pinyin Initials and Finals
rule.explanation: Pinyin uses roman letters to represent Chinese sounds. It is made up of an initial (consonant at the start) and a final (vowel part). For example, in 'ma', 'm' is the initial and 'a' is the final. Some common initials: b, p, m, f, d, t, n, l, g, k, h. Some common finals: a, o, e, i, u, ü.

rule.explanation: Chinese numbers 11–99 follow a simple pattern: say the tens digit + 十 (shí) + ones digit. For example, 十一 (shíyī) = 10+1 = 11, 二十 (èrshí) = 2×10 = 20, 三十五 (sānshíwǔ) = 3×10+5 = 35.

rule.title: Dates in Chinese
rule.explanation: Chinese dates go from largest to smallest: 年 (nián, year) → 月 (yuè, month) → 日/号 (rì/hào, day). Months are simply number + 月: 一月 = January, 二月 = February, etc. Days of the week use 星期 (xīngqī) + number: 星期一 = Monday.

rule.title: Direction Complements (进来, 出去, 回来, 上去)
rule.explanation: Direction complements are added after verbs to indicate the direction of movement. 来 (lái) means movement toward the speaker, 去 (qù) means movement away from the speaker. Common pairs: 进来/进去 (come in/go in), 出来/出去 (come out/go out), 回来/回去 (come back/go back), 上来/上去 (come up/go up).
